title: Cap. 6 Arg. 8: Broad-sense grace—natural light, creatures, outward benefits, inward motions
pass_a_gloss: Thus that natural light by which God enlightens every human being coming into the world, that testimony of the creatures by which the Gentiles are directed to some knowledge of the Creator, those external benefits by which God witnesses his philanthropy toward the whole world, those inward motions by which he sometimes affects the minds of the Gentiles so as either to restrain them from some evil work or to stir them to some good work—these can in this broad sense claim for themselves the name of grace. Under this general notion of grace the Pelagians hid the poison of their pestilent dogma. But neither do the Scriptures understand the grace given through Christ in that way, nor the holy Fathers, who after Pelagius arose learned to speak more cautiously.
pass_b_english: Natural light by which God lights every person who comes into the world; the witness of the creatures that steers the nations toward some knowledge of the Creator; outward benefits by which God shows his love of humankind to the whole world; inward stirrings that sometimes check a Gentile from evil or move him toward good—all these can, in that wide sense, wear the name grace. Under that blanket the Pelagians hid the poison of their teaching. Scripture does not mean the grace given through Christ that way, and neither do the holy Fathers once Pelagius forced them to speak more carefully.
source_text: Sic illud lumen naturale quo Deus illuminat omnem hominem venientem in mundum, illa creaturarum testificatio qua Ethnici ad aliquam Creatoris cognitionem diriguntur, illa beneficia externa quibus Deus suam φιλανθρωπίαν erga totum mundum testatur, illi interni motus quibus nonnunquam afficit animos gentilium, ut eos vel coerceat ab aliquo opere malo, vel excitet ad aliquod opus bonum, possunt hoc largo sensu gratiae nomen sibi vendicare. Pelagiani sub hac generali notione gratiae pestiferi sui dogmatis venenum occultarunt. Sed neque Scripturae gratiam per Christum datam ita intelligunt, neque sancti Patres, qui post exortum Pelagium cautius loqui didicerunt.
